newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-NEW COACH, OLD HOPES AND PLAYERS FOR BOCA.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-NEW COACH, OLD HOPES AND PLAYERS FOR BOCA.

text.p: The second and final championship of the Argentine soccer season begins at the weekend, allowing the country's most popular club Boca Juniors to once again revive their dreams of a return to greatness.

Hope springs eternal for Boca supporters, who for the past few years have believed the opening weekend of every competition will be the start of a revival, only to see their illusions shattered by around the halfway mark of the tournament.

This time last year, the return of Diego Maradona and coach Carlos Bilardo, the pair who led Argentina to World Cup victory in 1986 and the runners-up spot four years later, raised optimism and expectancy to an even higher level.
But Maradona missed a succession of penalties and abandoned the team, leaving Boca fans to watch formerly unfashionable Velez Sarsfield walk off with their third title in four years.
Bilardo did not give up and for the following tournament -- the 1996/7 Apertura championship which began in August -- the club spent a reported $15 million on building a completely new team.
Money, however, was not enough and despite the satisfaction of beating River Plate 2-1, Boca saw their arch-rivals win the championship by a nine-point margin.
Although Bilardo had said that he needed time to build a championship-winning team, Boca's fans demanded immediate success and the coach was out of the job in December.
Boca, a club with a huge tradition, have failed to win any of the last eight tournaments, which have been dominated by old foes River and upstarts Velez instead.

After the latest failure, president Mauricio Macri, a glamorous, young businessman who took over the club just over a year ago, announced an end to the big-spending approach and said Boca would concentrate on training promising youngsters.

"The model based on one or two magic players has not given good results," he said. As a result, the only major change for the Clausura championship has been the introduction of new coach Hector Vieira.
Two championships are played during the Argentine season, the Apertura (opening) from August to December and the Clausura (closing) from February to June.
The football itself tends to be overshadowed by the trials and tribulations of Boca, the antics of some of the goalkeepers and the controversies stirred up by hardline referee Javier Castrilli.
Three goalkeepers -- Paraguayan Jose Luis Chilavert of Velez, Ignacio Gonzalez of Racing Club and Carlos Bossio of Estudiantes -- got on the scoresheet in the Apertura.
Chilavert scored goals from free kicks and penalties, Gonzalez converted two penalties in one game and, not to be outdone, Bossio scored with a header.
Castrilli has upset many with his liberal use of the red card and is known as the lawman. Last week, he sent off three Uruguayans in a World Cup qualifying match in Ecuador.

River, the current South American champions who delighted many people with their attacking soccer in the Apertura, are hot favourites for the title with Boca, Velez, Independiente and Lanus seen as their main challengers.

Independiente were runners-up in the Apertura in their first championship under veteran coach Cesar Luis Menotti and could be an even bigger threat now that Menotti and his squad have got to know each other better.

Lanus, an unfashionable club from a Buenos Aires suburb, have never won a major title in Argentina but have enjoyed several relatively successful seasons and last year won the South American Conmebol Cup.
